newsitem.title: GERMANY: Commentators see politics in Stoiber's euro stance.
newsitem.headline: Commentators see politics in Stoiber's euro stance.

text.p: German commentators agreed on Monday Bavarian premier Edmund Stoiber's highly public campaign for a strict interpretation of the entry criteria for European minetary union really had little to do with the single currency.

The populist premier's stance had much more to do with raising his own personal political profile and showing his Christian Social Union (CSU) party standing up to Chancellor Helmut Kohl in Bonn ahead of regional state elections next year.

But editorialists also cautioned that the move could backfire badly for Stoiber, who is widely seen as taking a leaf out of the book of the late Franz Josef Strauss, his most illustrious predecessor as head of the southern state.

"Stoiber learned from Strauss how to raise the Bavarians' fears about decisions from Bonn and to make use of them," the liberal Sueddeutsche Zeitung said. "He knows it can pay off for a Bavarian head of government to make Kohl's life difficult."
Strauss, as both Bavarian premier and head of the CSU, the sister party of the chancellor's Christian Democratic Union, was often a thorn in Kohl's side in the 1970s and 1980s.
Stoiber's goal is to step into Strauss's shoes by securing the CSU leadership from Kohl's loyal finance minister Theo Waigel, to go along with his state premiership, commentators said.
"The fact he smashes some European policy china in the process doesn't bother Stoiber much," the Die Welt daily said.
"Waigel can sense Edmund Stoiber's euroscepticism is closer to the people. And that annoys him," said the Abendzeitung, the mass market daily in the Bavarian capital of Munich.
The Frankfurter Rundschau said Stoiber was likely to stick to his stance. "He won't simply knuckle under just because Helmut Kohl wrinkles his brow in annoyance," the paper said.

The liberal daily warned of danger for Kohl and Waigel if they decided not to rigidly apply the rule that single currency members must have a budget deficit of not more than three percent of gross domestic product.
"Stoiber would mobilise the CSU against this and presumably find a clear majority in favour of his stance," it predicted. "That would mean the end of the coalition in Bonn."
But Die Welt said Stoiber still had things to learn from his old party boss.
"Strauss, of course, always knew when he had to hold himself back not to endanger Bavarian interests. That sense of political judgment is still missing from Stoiber," it said.
The Sueddeutsche Zeitung said Stoiber, who wants a strong single currency, was playing a dangerous game by making common cause with nationalists who were against the euro altogether.
The paper said he had enough to do with domsetic Bavarian problems and recalled he had pledged to "tell the citizens where we're heading" when he took office in 1994.
"The Bavarians are heading out of paradise and the loud Edmund Stoiber, if he overstretches himself, is heading for oblivion," the Munich-based daily said.
